served.stem: A single base pair in the coding region of a gene is changed, yet the resulting polypeptide has exactly the same amino acid sequence as before. This type of mutation is called:
served.bankWhy: This tests whether you can carry a DNA change through the genetic code and out to the protein. The code is redundant, so several different codons spell the same amino acid, and a base swap that lands on one of those synonyms leaves the protein untouched. Sort the names by what the protein ends up doing: same protein is silent, one amino acid swapped is missense, an early stop is nonsense, and a shifted reading frame is a frameshift.

answer.line: The code has synonyms. A base swap that lands on another codon for the same amino acid leaves the protein untouched.

steps: Read what changed: one base pair, and the protein came out identical.
Know the code is redundant. Most amino acids have several codons, often differing only in the third base.
Name it by the protein. Same protein: silent. One amino acid swapped: missense. Early stop: nonsense.

choices.note: Missense is the next box over: the new codon spells a different amino acid, so the sequence changes. Here it did not.
The new codon is a synonym, so the same amino acid goes in.
A frameshift comes from inserting or deleting bases in a number not divisible by three. A single swap keeps the reading frame.
Nonsense is the case where the new codon is a stop, which cuts the protein short. This protein came out whole.
Transversion describes the swap itself, a purine for a pyrimidine. It says nothing about the protein, and the protein is what the stem asks about.
